    GHK-Cu for hair: what it is, what the studies show, how it is sold.

    Peptide Chooser editorial team. Checked 30 Oct 2026.

    Short answer

    The hair evidence for GHK-Cu is one lab study on follicles, done with a close relative, AHK-Cu.1 GHK-Cu is a small copper peptide that the body makes, sold in scalp serums and in research-use vials.2 Serums are cosmetics: legal to sell without FDA approval, and nobody has to show that they grow hair.3 Injectable GHK-Cu is not approved for any use.4

    What is GHK-Cu?

    GHK is a peptide of three amino acids (glycine, histidine and lysine). GHK-Cu is the same peptide carrying copper. The body makes it, and lab studies link it to skin repair and collagen.2

    Most of that work is in cells and animals. A 2026 review of the GHK-Cu research called the studies in people thin: most trials were small and tested face creams.6

    Is GHK-Cu FDA approved?

    No product with GHK-Cu is FDA approved for hair loss, or for anything else.4 How it may be sold depends on what it is sold as.

    As a serum or shampoo, it is a cosmetic. Cosmetics do not need FDA approval before they are sold, and the maker does not have to show that they work.3

    As a powder or vial, it is sold by research-use shops. A research-use label means the product is not meant for people.

    What do the studies show for hair?

    The study that hair pages quote, ours included, is from 2007. Researchers kept human hair follicles alive in a dish and added a copper peptide; the follicles grew longer and the cells at their base grew more.1

    Two things to know about it. The peptide was AHK-Cu, a close relative of GHK-Cu, not GHK-Cu itself.1 And a follicle in a dish is not a person: it tells you a peptide does something to cells, not that a serum on your scalp grows hair. We found no large trial of GHK-Cu for hair loss in people.

    Serum or injection: what is the difference?

    A serum goes on the scalp. It is a cosmetic, so its maker may sell it without proving any effect.3

    An injection is a vial of powder from a research-use shop, meant to be mixed and injected. It is not a medicine: no maker has sent the FDA the trial data that approval needs.7 We found no study in people that shows injected GHK-Cu grows hair. Our guide on injectable peptides for hair growth has more.

    What should you look for on a serum label?

    On a cosmetic label, the ingredients are listed from the largest amount to the smallest. Ingredients at 1% or less may follow in any order.8 So a copper peptide near the end of the list tells you little about how much is in the bottle.

    • Look for the name: GHK-Cu often appears as copper tripeptide-1.9
    • If the label or the maker states the amount, note it, so you can compare two serums.
    • A product meant to treat a disease or change how the body works is a drug under the law, even when it is sold as a cosmetic.3 So a serum that promises to treat hair loss is making a drug claim.
    • Before and after photos and "clinically tested" are marketing until you see the study.

    What does GHK-Cu cost?

    A scalp serum with copper peptides costs about $48 for 30 mL (Divi Scalp Serum).5

    A low price per mg is not a sign of quality. Our guide on how to read a COA shows what a lab report can and cannot tell you.

    None of this is medical advice. A doctor or dermatologist can tell you which option fits your hair loss.
